facts.statement: Fossils of Ctenacanthus have been discovered in the Bloyd Formation of Arkansas and the Cleveland Shale of Ohio, as well as in South America.
facts.quote: Remains have been found in the Bloyd Formation (Carboniferous Period) of Arkansas and the Cleveland Shale (Devonian Period) of Ohio in the United States and in South America.

facts.statement: Ctenacanthus lived from the Emsian to the Changhsingian stages, spanning approximately 410.62 to 251.902 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Emsian to Changhsingian (410.62 to 251.902 million years ago)

facts.statement: Ctenacanthus is classified within the family Ctenacanthidae and the class Chondrichthyes.
facts.quote: Parent group: Ctenacanthidae Family: Ctenacanthidae Class: Chondrichthyes

facts.statement: The genus Ctenacanthus was first described by Louis Agassiz in 1837.
Analysis of tooth wear in Ctenacanthus concinnus suggests it was an opportunistic feeder that consumed various prey, including other cartilaginous fish and ectocochleate cephalopods.
facts.quote: Dental microwear texture analysis (DMTA) of C. concinnus teeth shows that the species was an opportunistic feeder that would have eaten a variety of animals, including other chondrichthyans and ectocochleate cephalopods.

rejected.statement: Ctenacanthus is an extinct genus of cartilaginous fish belonging to the order Ctenacanthiformes, named for its comb-like spines.
rejected.quote: Ctenacanthus (from Greek, 'comb' and Greek, 'spine') is an extinct genus of ctenacanthiform chondrichthyan.
